  • a simple HTML quiz/form that asks a series of questions
  • checkboxes, radio buttons, and inputs get submitted at the end
  • based on the options selected and content added, output a CSS stylesheet

To do this you're going to basically either be switching between pre-written CSS classes, or else using the input right as content inside the CSS. Think of this:

  • Radio buttons: Pick a font-style {serif, sans-serif}

You can have two rules ready, and just give them the one they want. Maybe you have:

body { font-family: serif; }

and 

body { font-family: sans-serif; }

What advice would you have for a junior web guy to migrate to native developer from web?

I've been learning about web design and development for about 2 years, and have been employed for about 1,5 years in the field. Goes without saying, I am still very green. I am already quite uninterested in this particular field as it seems to be for more complicated, unstable, and underestimated than other more traditional programming fields.

Skippable Rant: Every month or so I have to learn the next cool build tool, front end framework or javascript/css preprocessor. It is a horrendously complicated and hipstery landscape. Furthermore, none of my colleagues seem to have any appreciation of how time-consuming tying all these little, ever-changing tools is. I'm expected to juggle and mix different frameworks with different philosophies and models, and also design new elements and style them perfectly. My job is perceived as easy, 'anyone can write HTML markup and CSS'. The reality of my job is completely misunderstood and undervalued. If there's an aspect of something that I don't get, the response is 'oh, we thought you were a full-stack dev'. What I'm experiencing is a fairly documented phenomenon for 'web designers' , it's sometimes called framework fatigue.

I am very passionate creator, and have an extensive list of projects which I intend to do at one point or another.

Some of these are web projects, though most of them are aimed at native mobile and desktop environments. The mobile apps I wish to create involve the camera and computer vision. The desktop apps I wish to create involve local headless file servers, additions the right-click menu in the native file managers, and binding new hotkeys

I get the impression that I could use python for all of these requirements. what do you recon?

Ultimately, I want to get closer to my projects, and worry less about the tools.
Transition to Native developer from web

You can pretty much use python for all of that, but to expand out, I'd suggest picking up some C. Its similar to python but without the pretentiousness, and you can use it to do the heavy lifting in python as extensions. Other people will suggest C++, but to be honest I think you should really master C's nuances before moving on, because it will make you a much better programmer.

In my work, web stuff comes up from time to time. I'm convinced that it has been made more difficult than it ought to be in order to keep the barrier to entry high. The number of frameworks and approaches is out of control.

The scary thing is that none of it works particularly well and no one has figured out the best way to do thing.

yeh its ridiculous.. every the tiniest web project is expected to use the latest proprietary technologies from facebook or google (reactjs or angular) which are designed for million-user applications, or some other behemoth application framework like backbone..
